analysis.one_liner: Imposes child-safety rules and audits on big online platforms and lets users switch off algorithmic feeds.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the final version 91-3 in July 2024, but the House never voted on that version, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill started as a small good-government measure from Senator Ossoff requiring agencies to list outdated, duplicative reports in their budget requests. Along the way it became the vehicle for a much larger package: the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act, which would require major social media, gaming, and streaming platforms to take 'reasonable care' against harms to minors, provide default safety controls and parental tools, publish annual third-party audits of risks to children, ban targeted advertising aimed at anyone under 17, and let users switch to a feed that does not use their personal data. The Senate approved that final version 91-3, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children and teens who use online platforms: parents get default-on safety controls, purchase limits, and time limits, and platforms must be audited and disclose risks to minors. All users also gain the right to see content ranked without their browsing and location data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents, teens, and everyday platform users

how_it_helps.text: Platforms likely used by minors must exercise reasonable care in design features to prevent anxiety, depression, eating disorders, addiction-like use, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to minors.

Platforms must give minors default-on safeguards (limits on contact, public personal data, compulsive design features like infinite scroll, recommendation systems, and location tracking) and give parents tools to manage privacy, purchases, and screen time.

Platforms averaging more than 10 million US users must publish yearly public reports based on an independent third-party audit of risks to minors, their mitigation steps, and their commercial interests in use by minors.
Under an updated children's privacy law, platforms may not collect, use, or disclose a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific (targeted) advertising.

Users of online platforms must be able to easily switch from an opaque algorithm (one that ranks content using their browsing history, inferences, and other unrequested data) to an input-transparent feed, with no price penalty for choosing the transparent option.
The original core of the bill requires agencies to list outdated or duplicative reporting requirements in their annual budget justifications, with recommendations to end, modify, or consolidate them.

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms — social networks, video games with in-game purchases, and streaming services — bear design changes, audit costs, and the loss of targeted advertising and engagement-driven revenue from minors. Advertisers lose a channel for reaching children. Users could face more collection of personal data as platforms infer ages, since the bill requires a study of age verification rather than mandating it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major tech platforms and online advertisers

drawbacks.text: Civil-liberties groups argue the 'duty of care' could pressure platforms to suppress lawful content — on mental health, LGBTQ topics, or abortion — to avoid liability for contributing to listed harms, chilling speech for minors and adults alike.

To comply, platforms may need to collect more personal data to infer who is a minor; the bill directs agencies to study device-level age verification precisely because forcing verification now would create privacy and data-security risks it does not yet solve.

The compliance burden falls unevenly: platforms under 10 million US users are exempt from the audit requirement, and the bill itself instructs the age-verification study to consider whether such systems create barriers to entry for small companies — meaning the rules could tilt the market toward incumbents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer wins are concrete: default safety controls for minors, independent audits of child-safety risks at the biggest platforms, a ban on targeted ads to children and teens, and an opt-out from algorithmic feeds. The honest objections are also real: the duty-of-care standard gives platforms a reason to over-remove lawful content, enforcement may push more data collection to determine ages, and compliance costs favor large incumbents over startups. A well-designed version would need stronger safeguards against censorship side effects and a real answer on age verification.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate rewrote the small reports bill into the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act and passed it 91-3, but the House never voted on that version before the 118th Congress ended, so the bill died.

narrative.text: Senator Ossoff introduced the Eliminate Useless Reports Act on June 21, 2023, requiring agencies to list outdated or duplicative reporting requirements in their budget justifications.
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee reported the bill favorably on August 22, 2023, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate passed the original bill by unanimous consent on December 18, 2023.
The House passed its own amended version by voice vote under suspension of the rules on May 6, 2024.

The Senate then concurred in the House amendment with a sweeping amendment (SA 3021) that replaced the bill's text with the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act — the combined Kids Online Safety and children's privacy provisions plus the reports sunset.
The Senate invoked cloture on the motion to concur 86-1 on July 25, 2024, and passed the final version 91-3 on July 30, 2024, with Democrats, Republicans, and Independents overwhelmingly in favor.
The House received the Senate's action on July 31, 2024, and took no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major online platforms — social media, gaming, and targeted-advertising companies — avoided new child-safety duties, mandatory third-party audits, and a ban on targeted ads to minors. The House leadership also avoided holding a vote on a controversial bill late in the session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media, gaming, and adtech firms

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: cloture passed 86-1 and final passage 91-3, with 43 of 47 voting Democrats, 44 of 49 voting Republicans, and all 4 Independents in favor; the only opposition came from 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

industries.industry: Major social media platforms (over 10 million US users)
industries.note: They would face a legal duty to prevent harms to minors, default-on safety controls, annual independent audits, and transparency reports, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement. Their engagement-driven business model — addictive design features, targeted ads, and data-driven ranking — is exactly what the bill restricts. The audit threshold exempts smaller sites, so the cost lands mainly on incumbents, which could entrench them against startups.
An updated children's privacy law bans individual-specific advertising to anyone under 17, eliminating targeted-ad revenue from minors and the profiling infrastructure behind it.

Games with microtransactions are covered platforms: they must limit compulsive design features and in-game purchases to minors, provide parental purchase and time controls, and respond to harm reports within set deadlines.

Services whose content is provider-selected rather than user-generated get a lighter compliance path — age-rating access controls, ad safeguards, and parental settings — rather than the full audit regime, but still face new obligations where minors use them.
